questions.question: Ciprofloxacin: describe an associated adverse effect for each organ system.
questions.question_raw: Ciprofloxacin. Describe an associated effect with each organ system
questions.model_answer: a) QT-interval prolongation (potassium-channel blockade delaying repolarization), predisposing to torsades de pointes; also aortic aneurysm/dissection. b) Dysglycemia – both hypo- and hyperglycemia (quinolones stimulate pancreatic islet insulin release; most marked historically with gatifloxacin). c) Arthropathy/cartilage toxicity and tendinopathy (tendinitis/tendon rupture). d) CNS effects – headache, dizziness, insomnia, and rarely seizures (GABA-receptor displacement), psychosis/delirium, plus peripheral neuropathy that may be irreversible.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of resistance for each of the following?
questions.question_raw: What is the mechanism of resistance for the following:
questions.model_answer: a) VISA: cell-wall changes (no enterococcal van genes) - a thickened cell wall whose excess D-Ala-D-Ala termini trap vancomycin in the outer peptidoglycan layers ('decoy'/clogging), plus increased cell-wall turnover, decreased autolytic activity, increased positive cell-wall charge, and reduced Agr function (mediated by mutations in TCSs such as GraSR, VraSR, WalKR). b) Fluoroquinolones in S. pneumoniae: stepwise target mutations in DNA gyrase (gyrA) and topoisomerase IV (parC/parE), plus efflux (PmrA). c) Penicillin/ampicillin in E. faecium: low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP5 - overexpression and/or mutation reducing beta-lactam binding. d) GAS + erythromycin: (1) erm-mediated ribosomal target methylation (23S rRNA) giving the MLSB phenotype and (2) mef-mediated macrolide efflux pump.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the VISA mechanism is in the slice (pp. 378-379); the S. pneumoniae fluoroquinolone, E. faecium PBP5, and GAS erm/mef mechanisms are from established Mandell/antimicrobial resistance knowledge (other chapters).

cohort_answer.text: VISA: Increased cell wall turnover. Increased thickness of cell wall and cross linking of peptidoglycan. S. pneumo with moxifloxacin - DNA gyrase, Topoisomerase IV. GAS with erythromycin - Erm gene - methylation of target site (MLSB phenotype); mef gene - efflux pump. E. faecium w/ penicillin: altered PBP5 - Overexpression

questions.question: Post-antibiotic effect.
questions.question_raw: Post-antibiotic effect

parts.text: Name two classes of antibiotics which exhibit this phenomenon.

parts_raw.text: Name two classes of antibiotics which exhibit this phenomenon.

questions.model_answer: a) The post-antibiotic effect is the persistent suppression of bacterial growth that continues after short antimicrobial exposure once drug concentration has fallen below the MIC (a delay before the organism re-enters logarithmic growth); duration depends on the specific organism-drug combination, concentration, and exposure time. b) Aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones (both give a ~2-6 h PAE against gram-negative bacilli); carbapenems such as imipenem also produce a PAE against GNB, and beta-lactams generally show a PAE against gram-positive organisms.

cohort_answer.text: PAE = inhibition of bacterial growth following exposure to an antibiotic even after drug concentration falls below MIC, exhibited by delay before microorganisms re-enter log-growth in vitro. Possible mechanisms: nonlethal damage induced by the antimicrobial resulting in slow recovery; persistence of antimicrobial at bacterial binding sites (ribosomes, DNA gyrase) and periplasmic space. Specific microorganism-antimicrobial combination is most important factor influencing presence/duration of PAE, along with concentration and length of exposure. In human studies, aminoglycosides (extended PAE against GNB) effective with once-daily dosing. Classes exhibiting PAE: Aminoglycosides (PAE against GNB, lasts 2-6 hrs); Fluoroquinolones (PAE against GNB, lasts 2-6 hrs); beta-lactams generally do not exhibit PAE against GNB (except imipenem) but induce ~2hr PAE against GP organisms.

questions.question: Ciprofloxacin: name one adverse effect in each of the following categories.
questions.question_raw: Ciprofloxacin
questions.model_answer: a) QT-interval prolongation (risk of torsades de pointes); also aortic aneurysm/dissection. b) Dysglycemia (hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia). c) Tendinopathy – acute tendinitis/tendon rupture (and arthropathy/cartilage toxicity). d) Seizures (or peripheral neuropathy, which may be irreversible; CNS neuropsychiatric effects up to psychosis).

cohort_answer.text: Cardiovascular: QTc prolongation. Endocrine: Dysglycemia (both hyper and hypo). MSK: Connective tissue toxicity, particularly acute tendinitis and increased risk of aortic dissection. Neurologic: Peripheral neuropathy - may be irreversible; CNS: neuropsych up to toxic psychosis, can cause seizures

questions.question: Regarding fluoroquinolones.
questions.question_raw: Regarding fluoroquinolones:

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action?
What is the concern with using fluoroquinolones in pregnancy?
List SIX acute and possibly life-threatening adverse effects.

parts_raw.text: What is the mechanism of action?
What is the concern with using fluoroquinolones in pregnancy?
List SIX acute and possibly life-threatening adverse effects.

questions.model_answer: a) They rapidly inhibit bacterial DNA synthesis by inhibiting two type II topoisomerases – DNA gyrase (primary target in most gram-negatives) and topoisomerase IV (primary target in many gram-positives) – stabilizing the cleaved enzyme-DNA complex, blocking resealing of double-strand breaks and acting as topoisomerase poisons, leading to bactericidal killing. b) Concern for fetal cartilage/joint (arthropathy) toxicity, based on cartilage erosions seen in immature animals, so they are generally avoided in pregnancy. c) (1) QT prolongation with torsades de pointes/ventricular arrhythmia; (2) anaphylaxis/angioedema (hypersensitivity); (3) severe hypoglycemia (dysglycemia); (4) seizures; (5) aortic aneurysm/dissection; (6) fulminant hepatotoxicity/hepatic failure. [Also: tendon rupture, Clostridioides difficile colitis.]
questions.beyond_mandell: Pregnancy avoidance is inferred from the chapter's animal cartilage/arthropathy data; the specific contraindication wording is general teratology guidance.

questions.question: You are on the Pharmacy and Therapeutics committee. What factors determine whether you recommend addition of a new fluoroquinolone to the formulary?
questions.question_raw: Q14 (2004 PM). You're on P&T committee: what factors determine whether you recommend addition of a new fluoroquinolone to the formulary

parts.text: What factors determine formulary addition of a new fluoroquinolone?

questions.model_answer: (1) Added spectrum/efficacy not already covered by existing formulary agents (therapeutic gap, clinical-trial evidence of benefit/non-inferiority). (2) Safety/adverse-effect profile (frequency and severity – QT, dysglycemia, tendinopathy, drug interactions) and contraindications. (3) Cost/pharmacoeconomics relative to existing options. (4) Local resistance/stewardship impact (collateral selection of resistant organisms). (5) Pharmacokinetic advantages (oral bioavailability, dosing convenience) and accumulated post-marketing/real-world experience, including use in other jurisdictions.
questions.beyond_mandell: General formulary/P&T decision-making framework, not specific chapter content.

cohort_answer.text: Added spectrum not covered by existing formulary meds; cost; adverse effects (prevalence, frequency); additional benefit/efficacy in clinical trials; experience in other countries.

questions.question: Fluoroquinolones carry important toxicities. Describe their molecular target and mechanism of action, and name six acute, potentially life-threatening adverse effects.
questions.question_raw: Fluoroquinolones are the real silent killer.

parts.text: Describe the target and mechanism of action
Name six acute and potentially life-threatening adverse effects

parts_raw.text: Describe the target and mechanism of action
Name 6 acute and potentially life-threatening adverse effects

questions.model_answer:
a) Target/mechanism: Quinolones rapidly inhibit bacterial DNA synthesis by targeting two type II topoisomerases — DNA gyrase (GyrA/GyrB; primary target in most gram-negatives) and topoisomerase IV (ParC/ParE; primary target in many gram-positives). They bind the enzyme-DNA complex, block resealing of the double-strand break, and stabilize a covalent enzyme-DNA cleavage complex that becomes a barrier to the replication fork and is converted to lethal double-strand DNA breaks (topoisomerase-poison effect), producing bactericidal killing.
b) Six acute, potentially life-threatening adverse effects: (1) QT-interval prolongation with torsades de pointes/ventricular arrhythmia; (2) Clostridioides difficile–associated colitis; (3) seizures (CNS excitation via GABA-receptor displacement); (4) aortic aneurysm and dissection; (5) severe hypoglycemia (notably gatifloxacin); (6) anaphylactoid/hypersensitivity reactions (angioedema, anaphylaxis). (Exacerbation of myasthenia gravis and acute hepatotoxicity/hepatic failure are also acceptable.)

cohort_answer.text: Mechanism: Directly inhibit DNA synthesis; bind to DNA gyrase and DNA topoisomerase IV, generating DNA cleavage. Adverse effects: QT prolongation; Aortic aneurysm and dissection; C. difficile associated disease; Altered mental status - seizures; Myasthenia gravis exacerbation; Tendinopathy; Dysglycemia; Retinal detachment; Hypersensitivity reactions; Pseudotumor cerebri

questions.model_answer: 1) Fluconazole over caspofungin (fluconazole achieves high urinary/renal and CSF levels; echinocandins have negligible urinary penetration). 2) Doxycycline over TMP-SMX (doxycycline is not used to treat CDI and carries low risk of inducing CDI). 3) Valganciclovir over valacyclovir (valganciclovir/ganciclovir has potent anti-CMV activity; valacyclovir is poorly active against CMV). 4) Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem (carbapenems interact with anti-epileptics, lowering levels, so the non-carbapenem beta-lactam is preferred). 5) Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin (per exam key, for a CNS bacterial infection; ampicillin over cloxacillin is also defensible for Listeria meningitis). 6) Atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency).
questions.beyond_mandell: Antibacterial/antifungal pairings draw on general ID pharmacology/guidance rather than this antiviral chapter; only the CMV/herpesvirus activity claims are grounded in Mandell Ch. 46.

cohort_answer.text:
Acyclovir over valacyclovir: HSV meningitis/encephalitis.
Valganciclovir over valacyclovir: Herpes B treatment better activity, CMV treatment.
Famciclovir over acyclovir: Uncomplicated zoster (famciclovir higher oral bioavailability than acyclovir, dosed TID rather than 5 times daily).
Atovaquone over dapsone: G6PD deficiency, Toxoplasmosis.
Doxycycline over TMP-SMX: Someone on Ramipril and Spironolactone with MRSA infection may want Doxycycline over TMP/SMX given risk of hyperkalemia.
Fluconazole over caspofungin: Cryptococcus not covered by echinocandins, urinary or CNS infections.
Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate: CNS infections, disseminated histoplasmosis, suspected mucormycosis.
Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem: Enterococcus.
Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin: Anaerobic activity is best with moxi.
Metronidazole over clindamycin: Bacteroides fragilis, increasing clinda resistance.
Azithromycin over clarithromycin: Better for gram-negatives, esp. M catarrhalis and H flu.
Ampicillin over cloxacillin: Enterococci, Listeria.
Cefazolin over cloxacillin: Surgical prophylaxis, penicillin allergy, AIN, heart failure.

questions.question: For the following antibiotics, provide the mechanism of interaction with tacrolimus: ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, rifampin, clarithromycin.

parts.text: For the following antibiotics, provide the mechanism of interaction with tacrolimus: ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, rifampin, clarithromycin.

parts_raw.text: For the following antibiotics, provide the mechanism of interaction with tacrolimus: Cipro, Vori, Rifampin, Clarithromycin

questions.model_answer: Tacrolimus is a CYP3A4 substrate, so interactions reflect each drug's effect on CYP3A4. (1) Ciprofloxacin - weak/negligible CYP3A4 inhibition; little clinically significant effect on tacrolimus (monitor). (2) Voriconazole - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; markedly increases tacrolimus levels (tacrolimus dose reduction required). (3) Rifampin - potent inducer of hepatic/intestinal CYP3A4, decreasing tacrolimus AUC/levels and risking acute graft rejection; rifabutin (least enzyme induction) is preferred in transplant recipients. (4) Clarithromycin - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; increases tacrolimus levels.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ciprofloxacin, voriconazole and clarithromycin mechanisms are established pharmacology (Mandell rifamycin chapter covers only the rifampin/tacrolimus interaction and rifabutin as preferred alternative).

cohort_answer.text: Ciprofloxacin: no clear known interaction (immunologic effects postulated, unlikely clinically relevant). Voriconazole: likely inhibition of CYP3A4 leading to increased tacrolimus levels. Rifampin: suspected induction of CYP3A4 leading to decreased tacrolimus levels. Clarithromycin: strong CYP3A4 inhibition leading to increased tacrolimus levels.

questions.model_answer: (1) Rifampin | rivaroxaban - rifampin induces CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein, decreasing rivaroxaban concentration and anticoagulant effect. (2) Rifampin | amlodipine (or bisoprolol) - CYP3A4 induction lowers the calcium-channel/beta-blocker level, reducing antihypertensive efficacy. (3) Ciprofloxacin | calcium - polyvalent cation chelation reduces ciprofloxacin absorption (separate dosing). (4) Linezolid | sertraline - additive serotonergic effect (linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor); risk of serotonin syndrome.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ciprofloxacin-calcium chelation and linezolid-sertraline serotonin syndrome are established pharmacology; the rifamycin chapter lists rivaroxaban, calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers and linezolid among rifampin interactions (Table 27.2) but does not detail the non-rifampin mechanisms.

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin-Rivaroxaban: CYP3A4 strong inducers may decrease serum concentration of rivaroxaban. Rifampin-Sertraline: CYP3A4 strong inducers may decrease serum concentration of sertraline. Rifampin-Bisoprolol/Perindopril/Amlodipine: CYP3A4 strong inducers may decrease serum concentration. Linezolid-Metformin: MAOIs may enhance hypoglycemic effect. Linezolid-Sertraline: linezolid may enhance serotonergic effect of SSRIs, risk of serotonin syndrome. Ciprofloxacin-Metformin: quinolones may enhance/diminish hypoglycemic effect. Ciprofloxacin-Calcium: multivitamins/minerals may decrease serum concentration of quinolones (polyvalent cations decrease absorption). Also caution with QT-prolonging agents.

questions.model_answer:
a) Caspofungin over fluconazole - azoles inhibit CYP3A4 and interact with carbamazepine (altered levels/toxicity), whereas the echinocandin has minimal CYP interaction.
b) Atovaquone over dapsone - dapsone causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
c) Doxycycline over clindamycin - clindamycin is strongly associated with C. difficile, while doxycycline is neither a C. difficile therapy nor a notable inducer of it. (Metronidazole is a C. difficile treatment, so it does not fit "not used for treatment.")
d) Levofloxacin over moxifloxacin - levofloxacin is renally excreted with high urinary concentrations, whereas moxifloxacin achieves poor urinary levels.
e) Valganciclovir over acyclovir - ganciclovir/valganciclovir is active against CMV; acyclovir is not reliably.
f) Ceftriaxone over cefuroxime - ceftriaxone reliably penetrates the CNS and is a standard meningitis agent, whereas cefuroxime has been associated with delayed CSF sterilization/meningitis failures.

questions.question: Describe the specific mechanisms of action for the following anti-tubercular medications.
questions.question_raw: Describe the specific mechanisms of actions for the following anti-tubercular medications.
questions.model_answer: a) Isoniazid: inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, blocking mycobacterial cell wall synthesis (bactericidal). b) Rifamycins (rifampin/rifabutin/rifapentine): inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (beta-subunit, rpoB); human RNA polymerase is insensitive. c) Linezolid: oxazolidinone that inhibits initiation of bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit (antimycobacterial toxicity relates to inhibition of mitochondrial protein synthesis). d) Levofloxacin: inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase, the enzyme maintaining DNA supercoiling needed for chromosomal replication. e) Bedaquiline: a diarylquinoline that inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, becoming bactericidal over several days.

questions.question: For each of the following drugs, state whether it will increase, decrease, or have no effect on the tacrolimus level.

parts_raw.text: For each of the following state whether they will increase, decrease or have no effect on the tacrolimus level: Voriconazole, Ciprofloxacin, Clarithromycin, Rifampin

questions.model_answer: Tacrolimus is a CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein substrate. (1) Voriconazole - increase (potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; reduce tacrolimus dose ~two-thirds). (2) Ciprofloxacin - no significant effect (minimal CYP3A4 activity; at most a minor rise). (3) Clarithromycin - increase (strong CYP3A4 inhibitor). (4) Rifampin - decrease (potent CYP3A4/P-gp inducer).

questions.question: Describe the interaction of tacrolimus (a CYP3A4 substrate) with each of the following: ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, rifampin, clarithromycin.
questions.question_raw: Interactions of tacrolimus with: Ciprofloxacin, Voriconazole, Rifampin, Clarithromycin.

parts.text: Describe the interaction of tacrolimus (a CYP3A4 substrate) with each of the listed drugs.

parts_raw.text: Describe the interaction of tacrolimus (a CYP3A4 substrate) with each of the listed drugs.

questions.model_answer: (1) Ciprofloxacin - only weak CYP3A4 inhibition; minimal clinically important change in tacrolimus. (2) Voriconazole - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; substantially increases tacrolimus levels, requiring dose reduction. (3) Rifampin - potent CYP3A4/intestinal enzyme inducer; decreases tacrolimus AUC and levels, risking subtherapeutic immunosuppression and acute graft rejection; rifabutin (least CYP3A4 induction) is the preferred rifamycin in transplant patients. (4) Clarithromycin - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; increases tacrolimus levels.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ciprofloxacin, voriconazole and clarithromycin mechanisms are established pharmacology; the rifamycin chapter covers only the rifampin interaction and rifabutin as the preferred transplant alternative.

cohort_answer.text: Tacrolimus is a CYP3A4 substrate. Ciprofloxacin - weakly inhibits CYP3A4, may increase tacrolimus. Voriconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreases tacrolimus levels (strongest contraindication; rifabutin should be used instead of rifampin to avoid interaction and reduce risk of acute graft rejection). Clarithromycin (and other macrolides) - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus.

questions.question: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase testing in Plasmodium vivax infection, and fluoroquinolone effects on glucose metabolism.

parts.text: Why do you need to test for G6PD in Plasmodium vivax infection?
Describe the two proposed mechanisms of glucose metabolism alteration with fluoroquinolone antibiotics.

parts_raw.text: Why do you need to test for G6PD in P. vivax infection?
Describe the two proposed mechanisms of glucose metabolism alteration with fluoroquinolone antibiotics

questions.model_answer: a) P. vivax (and P. ovale) form dormant liver-stage hypnozoites; radical cure to prevent relapse requires an 8-aminoquinoline (primaquine or tafenoquine), and these are the only drugs active against hypnozoites. Both cause oxidant hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients and are contraindicated in severe G6PD deficiency, so G6PD activity must be documented before prescribing. b) (1) Increased pancreatic insulin release (stimulation of insulin secretion, e.g. by blockade of ATP-sensitive K+ channels on the beta cell) causing hypoglycemia; (2) potentiation/interaction with concomitant oral hypoglycemic agents (e.g. sulfonylureas such as glyburide), producing dysglycemia (both hypo- and hyperglycemia).
questions.beyond_mandell: Fluoroquinolone dysglycemia mechanisms are not in this malaria chapter; drawn from established pharmacology (FQ-induced insulin secretion and interaction with sulfonylureas).

cohort_answer.text: In P. vivax and P. ovale, the dormant hypnozoite liver stage needs to be eradicated; the 2 antimalarials with activity against hypnozoites are primaquine and tafenoquine, both of which can cause hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency. FQ glucose mechanisms: stimulate release of insulin; interaction with hyperglycemic agents (e.g. glyburide).

questions.question: You want to start an elderly man on multiple medications on linezolid, ciprofloxacin and rifampin. He is currently taking ASA, calcium, bisoprolol, ramipril, metformin, rivaroxaban, sertraline and acetaminophen. Outline the possible drug-drug interactions with each antibiotic.
questions.question_raw: Abx drug interactions. You want to start an old guy on multiple meds on linezolid, cipro, rifampin. He is currently taking ASA, calcium, bisoprolol, ramipril, metformin, rivaroxaban, sertraline, acetaminophen.

parts.text: Outline the possible drug-drug interactions with each antibiotic.

parts_raw.text: Outline the possible drug-drug interactions with each antibiotic – (2019)

questions.model_answer:
Linezolid: (1) sertraline - additive serotonergic effect (linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor), risk of serotonin syndrome; (2) metformin - possible enhanced hypoglycemic effect.
Ciprofloxacin: (1) calcium - polyvalent-cation chelation reduces ciprofloxacin absorption (separate dosing); (2) sertraline - additive QTc prolongation; (3) metformin - fluoroquinolones may alter glycemic control (hypo-/hyperglycemia).
Rifampin (CYP3A4/enzyme inducer, lowering concomitant drug levels): (1) rivaroxaban - reduced concentration/anticoagulant efficacy; (2) bisoprolol - reduced beta-blocker level; (3) acetaminophen - induction increases hepatotoxic metabolite, higher hepatotoxicity risk; (4) calcium - may reduce rifampin absorption.
questions.beyond_mandell: Linezolid-serotonin, ciprofloxacin chelation/QTc and metformin glycemic effects are established pharmacology; the rifamycin chapter (Table 27.2) grounds the rifampin interactions with anticoagulants, beta-blockers and analgesics.

cohort_answer.text: Linezolid-sertraline (serotonin syndrome, QT prolongation); Linezolid-metformin (hypoglycemia); Cipro-calcium (impaired cipro absorption); Cipro-sertraline (QTc prolongation and TdP, did not flag in interaction checker); Cipro-ASA (decreased absorption of cipro); Cipro-metformin (hypoglycemia); Rifampin-acetaminophen (increased risk hepatotoxicity); Rifampin-bisoprolol (CYP3A4 induction, decreased bisoprolol efficacy); Rifampin-calcium (decreased rifampin absorption); Rifampin-rivaroxaban (decreased rivaroxaban efficacy)

questions.question: Identify agents of each class that cause QTc prolongation (the same agent cannot be reused): two antibiotics, one antiparasitic, and one anti-tuberculous drug.
questions.question_raw: Identify agents of each class that cause QTc prolongation (cannot reuse the same agent): 2 antibiotics, 1 antiparasitic, 1 anti-TB

parts.text: One anti-tuberculous drug causing QTc prolongation

questions.model_answer:
a) Two antibiotics: (1) A fluoroquinolone — moxifloxacin (greatest QT effect; ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin less so) — blocks cardiac potassium channels, delays repolarization, and can precipitate torsades de pointes. (2) A macrolide — erythromycin (or azithromycin), also a QT-prolonging agent with which quinolone effects are additive.
b) One antiparasitic: quinine (alternatively chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine or mefloquine).
c) One anti-TB drug: bedaquiline (alternatively clofazimine).
questions.beyond_mandell: The quinolone chapter grounds only the antibiotics (fluoroquinolone and erythromycin/macrolide) for QT prolongation; the antiparasitic (quinine/chloroquine) and anti-TB (bedaquiline/clofazimine) agents are established QT-prolongers from general pharmacology/drug-safety references, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin, Azithromycin. Antiparasitic: Quinine, Sodium stibogluconate, Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine (also possible but rare ~5%). Anti-TB: Clofazimine, Bedaquiline, Linezolid.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of action of rifampin, isoniazid, linezolid, moxifloxacin, and bedaquiline.
questions.question_raw: Describe the mechanism of: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Linezolid, Moxifloxacin, Bedaquiline.
questions.model_answer: a) Rifampin: inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (beta-subunit, rpoB); human RNA polymerase is insensitive. b) Isoniazid: inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, blocking cell wall synthesis (bactericidal). c) Linezolid: oxazolidinone inhibiting initiation of bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit; mycobacterial toxicity reflects inhibition of mitochondrial protein synthesis. d) Moxifloxacin: inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (and topoisomerase IV), disrupting DNA supercoiling required for chromosomal replication. e) Bedaquiline: diarylquinoline that inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, becoming bactericidal over several days.

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, occurring as a result of drug binding in the polymerase subunit deep within the DNA/RNA channel, facilitating direct blocking of elongating RNA. Isoniazid: Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, interfering with cell wall synthesis, producing a bactericidal effect; also disrupts DNA, lipid, carbohydrate, and NAD synthesis/metabolism. Linezolid: Inhibits initiation of bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 23S rRNA component of the 50S ribosome (contains 5S rRNA, 23S rRNA, 34 proteins); also suppresses production of bacterial toxins such as Panton-Valentine leukocidin, alpha-hemolysin, and TSST-1. Moxifloxacin: Directly inhibits DNA synthesis; binds to DNA gyrase and DNA topoisomerase IV, generating DNA cleavage. Bedaquiline: Inhibits bacterial ATP synthase; ATP production is required for cellular energy production and its loss leads to inhibition of mycobacterial growth within hours
